I can't remember, has anyone tried writing a linter for instance diamonds?

Here's my attempt at the spec for one. Feedback appreciated, I'll try to implement this shortly:

For each declaration with the [instance] attribute whose return type is a class:

  1. Reduce the return type to expose the class name (handles reducible aliases like abbrev).
  2. Look up the class's parent info (StructureInfo.parentInfo) to find direct parent classes and their projection functions. (We use the metadata, not toX naming conventions, since not all toX fields are parent embeddings.)
  3. For each pair of distinct direct parents (P, Q), compute their full transitive ancestor sets (via getAllParentStructures).

  4. For each common ancestor A of P and Q:

    • Obtain a canonical projection path from P to A and from Q to A (via getPathToBaseStructure?).
    • Construct the composed expressions inst.toP.⟨path to A⟩ and inst.toQ.⟨path to A⟩ directly in MetaM.
    • Check definitional equality at reducible-and-instances transparency (withReducibleAndInstances (isDefEq lhs rhs)).

  5. Report all failures. Deduplicate normalized path pairs to avoid noise.

This seems related to the overlapping instances linter #35095 (which @Jovan Gerbscheid and I are working on), which is stalled for performance reasons. Namely, when finding the projections for a single instance, there's a point at which we check if a projection has been encountered already and, if so, ignore it (assuming there aren't instance diamonds), where I believe we could instead check definitional equality.

(Or, if I'm misremembering the internals, I don't think it would be too much of an alteration to change it to meet the spec above.)
(An environment linter for instance diamonds might not face the same performance issues, since it would just be running once for each instance.)

I think it's not directly related: I'm asking about individual instances that have non-instance-defeq paths to ancestors.

I think it's probably best to keep this separate from finding overlapping instances in the context.

I wrote a little environement linter that searches for instances whose definition abuses defeq:

module
public import Mathlib
public meta section

open Lean Meta
namespace Batteries.Tactic.Lint

def checkInstance (cinfo : ConstantInfo) : MetaM (Option MessageData) := do
  let type := cinfo.type
  let some cls ← Meta.isClass? type | return none
  if cls matches
    ``Decidable | ``DecidableEq | ``DecidableLT | ``DecidableLE |
    ``Inhabited | ``Unique | ``Unitization then
    return none
  if ← isProp type then return none
  let some value := cinfo.value? | return none
  let constants := Expr.getUsedConstants type
  if constants.any (· matches
    ``OrderDual | ``Additive | ``Multiplicative | ``Lex | ``Colex) then
    return none
  withReducibleAndInstances do
  let type' ← inferType value
  if ← isDefEq type' type then return none
  forallTelescope type fun _ type =>
  forallTelescope type' fun _ type' =>
  return some <| ← addMessageContext m!"{indentExpr type'}{indentExpr type}\n"

@[env_linter] public def myLinter : Linter where
  noErrorsFound := "all good."
  errorsFound := "PROBLEM"
  test declName := do
    checkInstance (← getConstInfo declName)

I filtered out some common classes and type synonyms, to make the output a bit more manageable. Here's the output on current mathlib, finding 796 bad instances:

instance addMonoidWithOne : AddMonoidWithOne (WithBot α) :=

#37195 cleans up OrderDual instances. Many of the instances had the form

instance [h : CommSemigroup α] : CommSemigroup αᵒᵈ := h

But I instead changed then to be made using the where notation, filling in all of the fields. This way, the leakyness is localized to data fields such as in LE and Mul. As long as the lambda binders there have the right type, this leakyness is not problematic.

This is a clear improvement, but I wonder if it wouldn't be better to have a version of inferInstanceAs or fast_instance% do this, instead of doing it by hand. This would involve recursing through the subclasses until the data fields, and using the already registered instances whenever possible, something that these tools already do.

Yes, I agree it would make sense to have tool to do this automatically. The one part that is different from what the current tools do, is that they only reduce a given instance to its constructor. But what we need here, is to create the constructor "out of thin air" (or more precisely, by doing structure eta expansion).

I'd like to help review some of these PRs to get them in quicker, but will I need to study the way instance synthesis works first, or are these supposed to be fairly trivial?

I'll try to give a summary.

Some of the set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false are good, in the sense that there is obviously a step in the proof that is abusing some definitional equality.

However, there are other cases, where type class search unification fails. For these you have to look deeply into the isDefEq traces to figure out what is going wrong. These are caused by instances not being definitionally equal to eachother in the reducible_and_instances transparency. This is often caused by the implicit type arguments being different, in which case the inferInstanceAs/fast_instance% machinery helps to fill in the correct types. But there can also be other reasons why these instance diamonds can appear.

So it's not really that instance synthesis works differently. Instead, it got pickier about what it wants to unfold and unify.
Is it the case that using inferInstanceAs / fast_instance% always leads to better terms if they succeed or did those have to be verified carefully when making the PR?

The standard use case are the following. Say, you have a type α and a synonym Copy α. If typeclass inference knows how to infer a class Foo α, then the good phrasing to get the same instance on Copy α is

instance : Foo (Copy α) := inferInstanceAs <| Foo α

That's always good, no need to check.

I don't think there can be any negative effects from using inferInstanceAs and fast_instance%.

One edge-case could be that you explicitly want your instance to be leaky, because making it non-leaky would require a bigger refactor. But this should not be common.
Thanks! That's very helpful!

Say also that you have a definition giving an instance of the class Foo α, called myNiceDef α, not registered for typeclass inference. Then the correct way to use it to endow Copy α is

instance : Foo (Copy α) :=
  fast_instance% myNiceDef α

Another version, which is slightly less nice, is

instance : Foo (Copy α) :=
  letI : Foo α := myNiceDef α
  inferInstanceAs <| Foo α

It's more verbose, but sometimes it works while fast_instance% doesn't.

Again, those spellings are very safe, no need to double-check what they output.

I'll have to look into the case where fast_instance% fails.

Note that there are subtle differences in how fast_instance% and inferInstanceAs normalize. This is a side-effect of inferInstanceAs being upstreamed to core, with a few modifications from the mathlib implementation. I should also look into fixing this discrepancy.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Yes, I agree it would make sense to have tool to do this automatically. The one part that is different from what the current tools do, is that they only reduce a given instance to its constructor. But what we need here, is to create the constructor "out of thin air" (or more precisely, by doing structure eta expansion).

(Where) is it relevant that the new instance reduces up to the lambda body of fields, i.e. more than

instance [CommSemigroup α] : CommSemigroup αᵒᵈ := inferInstanceAs <| CommSemigroup α

would?

Here is an example that fails on current master (but will succeed there soon)

module

public import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.Defs
public import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.GroupWithZero.Action.Synonym
public import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Ring.Synonym

variable {α β : Type*}

set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true in
set_option trace.Meta.isDefEq true in
instance instModule [Semiring α] [AddCommMonoid β] [Module α β] : Module αᵒᵈ β where
  add_smul := add_smul (R := α)
  zero_smul := zero_smul _

And here's a relevant part of the trace

[Meta.synthInstance] ❌️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
  [] ✅️ new goal DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▶
  [apply] ✅️ apply @OrderDual.instDistribMulAction to DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
    [tryResolve] ✅️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ≟ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
      [isDefEq] ✅️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β =?= DistribMulAction ?m.10ᵒᵈ ?m.11 ▼
        [] ✅️ αᵒᵈ =?= ?m.10ᵒᵈ ▶
        [] ✅️ β =?= ?m.11 ▶
        [] ✅️ inst✝¹.toAddMonoid =?= ?m.13 ▶
        [] ✅️ instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid =?= instMonoidOrderDual ▼
          [] ✅️ instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid =?= ?m.12 ▼
            [] instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid [nonassignable] =?= ?m.12 [assignable]
            [] ✅️ Monoid α =?= Monoid αᵒᵈ ▶
      [isDefEq] ✅️ ?m.9 =?= OrderDual.instDistribMulAction ▶
    [] ✅️ new goal DistribMulAction α β ▶
  [apply] ❌️ apply @Module.toDistribMulAction to DistribMulAction α β ▶

What is happening here is that Lean successfully applies OrderDual.instDistribMulAction, and during that unification, it unifies the instance parameters that have type Monoid αᵒᵈ. One of the two is given by instMonoidOrderDual applied to ?m.12, while the other is instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid. Lean then unfolds the leaky instance instMonoidOrderDual, at which point things start falling appart.

Now, if we had used inferInstanceAs, the leaky instance would not have been unfolded, which is good. But, in that case the unification just fails immediately:

[Meta.synthInstance] ❌️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
  [] ✅️ new goal DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▶
  [apply] ❌️ apply @OrderDual.instDistribMulAction to DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
    [tryResolve] ❌️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ≟ DistribMulAction ?m.10ᵒᵈ ?m.11 ▼
      [isDefEq] ❌️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β =?= DistribMulAction ?m.10ᵒᵈ ?m.11 ▼
        [] ✅️ αᵒᵈ =?= ?m.10ᵒᵈ ▶
        [] ✅️ β =?= ?m.11 ▶
        [] ✅️ inst✝¹.toAddMonoid =?= ?m.13 ▶
        [] ❌️ instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid =?= instMonoidOrderDual ▼
          [] ❌️ instSemiringOrderDual.toMonoidWithZero.1 =?= instMonoidOrderDual ▼
            [] ❌️ { toMul := instSemiringOrderDual.toMul, mul_assoc := ⋯, toOne := instSemiringOrderDual.toOne, one_mul := ⋯,
                  mul_one := ⋯, npow := Semiring.npow, npow_zero := ⋯, npow_succ := ⋯ } =?= instMonoidOrderDual ▼
              [] ✅️ Monoid αᵒᵈ =?= Monoid αᵒᵈ
              [] ❌️ instMonoidOrderDual.toSemigroup =?= { toMul := instSemiringOrderDual.toMul, mul_assoc := ⋯ } ▼
                [] ❌️ instMonoidOrderDual.1 =?= { toMul := instSemiringOrderDual.toMul, mul_assoc := ⋯ } ▼
                  [] ✅️ Semigroup αᵒᵈ =?= Semigroup αᵒᵈ
                  [] ❌️ instMonoidOrderDual.1.toMul =?= instSemiringOrderDual.toMul ▼
                    [] ❌️ instMonoidOrderDual.1.1 =?= instSemiringOrderDual.toNonUnitalNonAssocSemiring.2 ▼
                      [onFailure] ❌️ instMonoidOrderDual.1.1 =?= instSemiringOrderDual.toNonUnitalNonAssocSemiring.2

If the instance is given this artifical eta expansion, the trace looks like this:

[Meta.synthInstance] ✅️ DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▼
  [] ✅️ new goal DistribMulAction αᵒᵈ β ▶

        [] ✅️ αᵒᵈ =?= ?m.10ᵒᵈ ▶
        [] ✅️ β =?= ?m.11 ▶
        [] ✅️ inst✝¹.toAddMonoid =?= ?m.13 ▶
        [] ✅️ instSemiring.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid =?= instMonoid ▼
          [] ✅️ instSemiring.toMonoidWithZero.toMonoid =?= { toSemigroup := instSemigroup, toOne := instMulOneClass.toOne,
                one_mul := ⋯, mul_one := ⋯, npow := Monoid.npow, npow_zero := ⋯, npow_succ := ⋯ } ▼
            [] ✅️ instSemiring.toMonoidWithZero.1 =?= { toSemigroup := instSemigroup, toOne := instMulOneClass.toOne, one_mul := ⋯,
                  mul_one := ⋯, npow := Monoid.npow, npow_zero := ⋯, npow_succ := ⋯ } ▼
              [] ✅️ { toMul := instSemiring.toMul, mul_assoc := ⋯, toOne := instSemiring.toOne, one_mul := ⋯, mul_one := ⋯,
                    npow := Semiring.npow, npow_zero := ⋯,
                    npow_succ :=
                      ⋯ } =?= { toSemigroup := instSemigroup, toOne := instMulOneClass.toOne, one_mul := ⋯,
                    mul_one := ⋯, npow := Monoid.npow, npow_zero := ⋯, npow_succ := ⋯ } ▼
                [] ✅️ Semiring.npow =?= Monoid.npow ▼
                  [] ❌️ @Semiring.npow =?= @Monoid.npow
                  [onFailure] ✅️ Semiring.npow =?= Monoid.npow ▼
                    [stuckMVar] found stuck MVar ?m.12 : Monoid α
                    [synthInstance] ✅️ Monoid α ▶

The magic trick is that we managed to convince lean that the metavariable ?m.12 : Monoid α is stuck, so that is has to be synthesized.

I would guess we actually want something more like this?

import Mathlib

open Lean Elab Meta
partial def etaExpandStructure (e : Expr) : MetaM Expr := do
  let type ← whnf (← inferType e)
  let .const structName us := type.getAppFn
    | return e -- Base case: not a structure type
  let env ← getEnv

  if ¬ isStructure env structName then
    return e -- Base case: name isn't registered as a structure

  let ctorVal := getStructureCtor env structName

  if e.isAppOf ctorVal.name then
    return e

  let typeArgs := type.getAppArgs
  let mut res := mkAppN (Expr.const ctorVal.name us) typeArgs
  let fields := getStructureFields env structName

  for field in fields do
    let some info := getFieldInfo? env structName field
      | throwError "Failed to find field {field} for {structName}"
    let some projInfo ← getProjectionFnInfo? info.projFn
      | throwError "Failed to find projection info for {info.projFn}"

    -- Blindly slice arguments to build the projection
    let projArgs := (typeArgs.extract 0 projInfo.numParams).push e
    let projApp := mkAppN (Expr.const info.projFn us) projArgs

    -- 🔄 Recursion: Deeply expand this field projection!
    let expandedField ← etaExpandStructure projApp
    res := mkApp res expandedField

  return res

elab "eta_struct%" e:term : term <= ty => do
  let e ← Lean.Elab.Term.elabTerm e ty
  etaExpandStructure e

def Copy (α : Type) := α

namespace Copy




open Qq


instance [CommSemigroup α] : CommSemigroup (Copy α) := fast_instance% (eta_struct% ‹CommSemigroup α›)
instance [CommMonoid α] : CommMonoid (Copy α) := fast_instance% (eta_struct% ‹CommMonoid α›)

end Copy

#print Copy.instCommMonoid
I think probably fast_instance% could be modified to allow non-constructors, perhaps as fast_instance%!, and do the eta-expansion internally

Yes, I was thinking that we could have a boolean option to fast_instance% which does the eta expansion.

Though maybe a more fundamental question is whether we really need the eta expansion. Maybe this can be fixed in the unification algorithm, by improving the findStuckMVar function.

Here's a curious case of an instance diamond: There's two different ways in which ℂ can be a ℝ algebra, using either of

Algebra.complexToReal {A : Type*} [Semiring A] [Algebra ℂ A] : Algebra ℝ A
Complex.instAlgebraOfReal {R : Type*} [CommSemiring R] [Algebra R ℝ] : Algebra R ℂ

This leads to the following funny situation:

import Mathlib
-- Uncomment this line to swap which of the below cases succeeds:
-- attribute [-instance] Complex.instNormedAlgebraOfReal Complex.instRCLike

variable {R} [Field R] [Algebra ℂ R] in
#synth IsScalarTower ℝ ℂ R -- fails

variable {R} [NormedField R] [NormedAlgebra R ℝ] in
#synth IsScalarTower R ℝ ℂ -- succeeds
are they defeq at default transparency

We see lots of a generalized version of this in algebraic number theory, where we have fields K and L which are fixed in an entire file with Algebra K L, and then later on we want to go from Algebra L X to Algebra K X, but the way this is usually dealt with is: don't ask typeclass inference to find Algebra K X for you, but instead just add assumptions [Algebra K X] [IsScalarTower K L X]. This is why we end up with 5-line variable commands but it avoids this issue. You can see that people are aware that both docs#Algebra.complexToReal and docs#Complex.instAlgebraOfReal are hacks because they have reduced priority. Increased priority is not a hack, it is "this is bound to be what we want if it works so let's try it first". Reduced priority is a hack -- it means "this might screw things up so let's try it last and just hope".

An analogous situation is when I make a new module for a topological ring and I want to give it the module topology. I don't write instance : TopologicalSpace M := ModuleTopology R M, I write [TopologicalSpace M] [IsModuleTopology R M].

Would the real/complex analysts be interested in this fix? It would involve removing both instances and then adjusting a bunch of code. Or perhaps removing just one of them. To be honest, docs#Complex.instAlgebraOfReal looks pretty weird to me -- how often does a ring R fall out of the sky with an Algebra R ℝ instance? This is in stark contrast to rings falling out of the sky with Algebra ℂ A instances -- there are lots of these (function spaces, Banach algebras etc).

I wonder if we could some kind of "continuation passing style" trick to define the instances such that the scalar towers definitionally associate, using the fact that function composition is definitionally associative.

I wrote a linter to detect instance diamonds. There are 2 kinds of diamonds: diamonds that do not unify in reducible_and_instances transparency but do unify in default, and diamonds that do not even unify in default. The former is what causes the respectTransparency problems. The latter are pre-existing diamonds.

  • Diamonds that do unify in default: 224 found: https://gist.github.com/JovanGerb/014c0384cc20b7bcea1b497519171568
  • Diamond that don't unify in default: 23 found: https://gist.github.com/JovanGerb/9719c1f5ec6cbb607a457f6478039d0e

Implementation

module
public import Mathlib

public meta section

open Lean Meta

/-- Given an instance `inst`, return all data projection instances (e.g. `inst.toAddMonoid`). -/
partial def getStructureDataProjections (e : Expr) (acc : Array Expr := #[]) :
    StateRefT NameSet MetaM (Array Expr) := do
  let eType ← whnf (← inferType e)
  if ← isProp eType then return acc
  let .const structName us := eType.getForallBody.getAppFn
    | throwError "{e} is not an instance of a structure"
  unless isClass (← getEnv) structName do return acc
  if (← get).contains structName then return acc
  modify (·.insert structName)
  let some info := getStructureInfo? (← getEnv) structName | return acc
  info.parentInfo.foldlM (init := acc.push e) fun acc info ↦ do
    if ← isInstance info.projFn then
      let proj := Expr.app (mkAppN (.const info.projFn us) eType.getAppArgs) e
      getStructureDataProjections proj acc
    else
      return acc

/-- Compare the given instance with the one generated by type class synthesis. -/
def compareWithSynthesized (e : Expr): MetaM (Option MessageData) := do
  let type ← inferType e
  let .some inst ← trySynthInstance type | return none
  if ← withReducibleAndInstances <| isDefEq e inst then
    return none
  if ← withDefault <| isDefEq e inst then
    return m!"Projection {indentExpr e} : {← inferType e}\nis not defeq to the synthesized instance {indentExpr inst}"
  else
    return none

def findDiamonds (declName : Name) : MetaM (Option MessageData) := withReducible do
  unless ← isInstance declName do return none
  let cinfo ← getConstInfo declName
  let constants := Expr.getUsedConstants cinfo.type
  if constants.any (· matches ``Additive | ``Multiplicative |
      ``Lex | ``Colex | ``DomAddAct | ``DomMulAct | ``MulOpposite | ``AddOpposite
      | ``RestrictScalars | ``WithVal) then
    return none
  forallTelescopeReducing (whnfType := true) cinfo.type fun xs _ ↦ do
    let inst := mkAppN (.const declName (cinfo.levelParams.map .param)) xs
    let mut firstMsg : Option MessageData := none
    let mut later : Array Expr := #[]
    logInfo "fjiosd"
    for proj in ← (getStructureDataProjections inst).run' {} do
      logInfo m!"{proj}"
      if let some msg ← compareWithSynthesized proj then
        if firstMsg.isNone then
          firstMsg := some msg
        else
          later := later.push proj
    firstMsg.mapM fun msg ↦ do
      let mut msg := msg
      if !later.isEmpty then
        msg := m!"{msg}\nSimilarly for {later}"
      addMessageContext msg

namespace Batteries.Tactic.Lint

@[env_linter] def instanceDiamonds : Lint.Linter where
  noErrorsFound := "No problem"
  errorsFound := "Some problems"
  test := fun declName => do
    if declName.isInternal then return none
    findDiamonds declName

I have an interesting diamond, fixed in #38481 but I guess it appears a lot of times throughout Mathlib.

The diamond is the following. If a space E is a C-module, then it is automatically an R-module (Module.complexToReal). Define now a type synonym E' to E, and declare that, if k acts on E, then it also acts on E', through inferInstanceAs. Then E' is a C-module (instance applied to k=C), and therefore an R-module by Module.complexToReal. But, as E is an R-module (by Module.complexToReal), then E' is also an R-module (by the instance applied to k=R). Sure we can hide everything away with categories. But when we don't, here's how to have a Galois group acting on both a finite extension of number fields and of their integer rings:

variable
    -- let K be a number field with ring of integers A
    {A K : Type*}
    [CommRing A] [IsDedekindDomain A]
    [Field K] [NumberField K] [Algebra A K]
    [IsFractionRing A K]
    [IsIntegralClosure A ℤ K]
    -- let L be a number field containing K
    {L : Type*} [Field L] [Algebra K L] [NumberField L]
    [Algebra A L] [IsScalarTower A K L]
    -- and let B be the integers of L (which of course contains A)
    {B : Type*} [CommRing B] [Algebra B L]
    [Algebra A B] [IsScalarTower A B L]
    [IsIntegralClosure B A L]
    -- Let G be the Galois group of L/K
    variable {G : Type*} [Group G]
    [MulSemiringAction G L]
    [SMulCommClass G K L]
    [Algebra.IsInvariant K L G]
    [MulSemiringAction G B]
    [SMulCommClass G A B]
    [Algebra.IsInvariant A B G]
    [IsScalarTower G B L]
    -- Then we can do stuff

My point was that instead of having instances saying "A is the integers of K and K acts on L so A acts on L" we say "assume A acts on L and that the triangle commutes". Similarly instead of saying "G acts on L so it acts on its integer ring B" we say "assume G acts on B and the triangle commutes". Whereas the analysts have taken a different path, they say "if C\mathbb{C}C acts on X then so does R\RR", so they get different problems.

And when these fields are local fields it will be even longer, because G will act on the local fields, the integer rings, and also the residue fields, meaning lots more assumptions of actions and their compatibilities. We just saw mathlib attempting to shortcut this with an instance Algebra A B -> Algebra (ResidueField A) (ResidueField B) and it runs into this deadly SMul X Y -> SMul (F X) (F Y) trap (which causes diamonds when e.g. X=Y), which Thomas Browning is sorting out in another thread (#mathlib4 > instance diamond with `Ideal.Fiber` @ 💬 )
